xperienced people into employment through a dedicated employability pathway and free online skills resources. Designed with input from people who have lived experience of care, the programme is available across all John Lewis Partnership locations.

The programme includes a welcome tour, job shadowing, interview skills training and an interview. Successful candidates are offered suitable vacancies where available. Those who pass the interview but cannot be placed immediately may join a talent pool for up to 3 months and be contacted when opportunities arise.

Care-experienced people who work for the organisation can join a dedicated colleague network led by people with lived experience, and dedicated wellbeing support is also available. Managers and workplace buddies involved in the programme complete Care Aware training, helping them understand the barriers care-experienced people may face and how to create a more supportive working environment. The organisation offers a wide range of opportunities to boost skills and help people progress, including apprenticeships.

A free online employability platform offers practical support, including CV writing and interview preparation.

Digital skills and online safety

The ability to navigate online spaces safely and confidently is essential for accessing education, employment, financial services, health information and social support. There is significant benefit from practical, non-judgmental training for care-experienced young people, particularly for those who have not benefited from peer or parental oversight on online safety previously.

Local authorities should consider, alongside what financial support can be offered for access to broadband, what support can be provided to care-experienced young people as part of their local offer, including in areas such as:

how to spot scams, phishing and deepfakes

understanding online grooming and exploitation behaviours

managing social media privacy settings

recognising online hate or radicalisation

safe use of dating apps and sharing images

protecting personal data, especially when applying for jobs or housing

Developing and publishing the local offer

This section contains details on:

developing the local offer with care-experienced people

recognising different identities and experiences

additional considerations when developing the local offer

publishing and updating the local offer

format of the local offer

Developing the local offer with care-experienced people

When developing their local offer, local authorities are required to consult with relevant persons, which means care-experienced young people, and organisations or people that represent and support care-experienced young people.

Local authorities should consider how best to engage and consult with as many of their care-experienced young people as possible. We expect local authorities to work with their care-experienced young people to co-produce a local offer that is meaningful and reflects the needs, views and wishes of the care-experienced young people they are responsible for.

Recognising different identities and experiences

Care leavers will differ in:

ethnicity

culture

religion

gender identity

sexual orientation

disability or neurodiversity

Recognising diversity ensures that services are inclusive and culturally competent.

Local authorities have obligations under the Equality Act 2010 to prevent discrimination and actively promote inclusion and fairness.

Local authorities should ensure that the local offer is shaped by input from care leavers from underrepresented groups, which will:

help the offer reflect real needs

ensure the offer is relevant and practical

empower young people to have a voice

Additional considerations when developing the local offer

Local authorities will want to consider what additional non-statutory support is required to meet the needs of their cohort of care-experienced young people.

The local offer must include, and should differentiate between, both care-experienced young people’s statutory entitlements and other additional support that local authorities choose to provide.

The local offer should:

reflect support offered by all local authority departments, not only children’s services, including housing, education, leisure services, public health, youth services, libraries, employment and skills, transport, welfare and financial support teams and community safety

include, as part of the offer, any discrete service provided by a partner organisation for care-experienced young people, such as a health drop-in exclusively for care-experienced young people, where the local authority is confident that there is an ongoing commitment from that organisation to provide that service or support

signpost or provide links to services provided by partner organisations that are available to all young people, such as a young people’s sexual health clinic or a careers advice service for 16 to 25 year-olds, where this is more appropriate. The local offer should also explain what support the local authority can provide to help care-experienced young people access those services – for example, help with making referrals, arranging appointments, accompanying them where appropriate or covering travel costs if needed

Publishing and updating the local offer

Once local authorities have consulted on and published their local offer, it must be updated from time to time and should be reviewed regularly to ensure that the services on offer reflect what care-experienced young people need most.

Local authorities can choose how regularly they review their local offer, but we would expect local authorities to update it at least every 2 years, following further consultation with care-experienced young people.

Local authorities should use the allowance flexibly to meet individual needs, including where young parents may require additional essential items for themselves and their child.

The local offer should clearly explain:

who is eligible for the allowance

how young people can access it

how it is administered, including whether support is provided through direct purchases, instalments or lump-sum payments

the types of items it can be used to fund

any local processes for requesting support

any additional discretionary financial assistance that is available beyond the statutory allowance

The local offer should distinguish between support provided through the statutory leaving care allowance and any additional discretionary assistance offered by the local authority.

Where goods or services are purchased on behalf of a young person using the leaving care allowance, the local offer should explain how decisions are made and how the allowance will be allocated. This will help ensure transparency and enable young people to make informed choices about how their entitlement is used.

Education and training entitlements, allowances and bursaries

The local offer should explain financial support available to young people participating in FE, HE and apprenticeships, including:

the £3,000 apprenticeship care leavers’ bursary

the 16 to 19 bursary fund

the £2,000 higher education bursary

information on extended eligibility for foundation apprenticeships and level 7 apprenticeships, from age 21 to 24, for care-experienced young people, prisoners and ex-prisoners and people with an education, health and care plan

any local grants, travel assistance, equipment funding or other discretionary support, including for interview or work clothing

Further information is included in education, training and employment.

Benefits and entitlements

The local offer should provide information about benefits and financial entitlements that may be available to care-experienced young people and explain what support is available to help them access those entitlements.

This should include information about:

Universal Credit

council tax support and exemptions

disability-related benefits and support

housing-related financial assistance

support available through education, employment or training

local welfare support schemes and discretionary financial assistance

The local offer should explain:

what support is available

who may be eligible

how applications can be made

what help is available to complete applications and navigate the benefits system

Some former care-experienced unaccompanied asylum-seeking children (UASC) may be unable to access benefits as a result of having a “No Recourse To Public Funds” condition on their immigration status.

The local authority should assess the needs of the young person and gain a full understanding of their individual circumstances. A human rights assessment under schedule 3 of the Nationality, Immigration and Asylum Act 2002 may need to be completed to determine which services should be provided. Schedule 3 of the Nationality, Immigration and Asylum Act 2002 sets out the entitlements which migrants with No Recourse to Public Funds can access.

Former UASC and migrant children leaving care includes further information.

Junior individual saving accounts (ISAs)

Children who have been looked after continuously for 12 months or more and who are not eligible for a Child Trust Fund are entitled to receive a government contribution of £200 into a junior ISA.

The local offer should explain:

what a junior ISA is

who may be entitled to one

how young people can find out whether an account exists in their name

how they can access the account when eligible to do so

where they can obtain support if account information has been lost or if they were not previously aware of the account

Local authorities should ensure that care-experienced young people are aware of junior ISAs and understand how these savings can support them as they move into adulthood.

Case study: example of local practice

Derbyshire’s local offer provides practical, structured financial support to help care leavers manage money and transition to independence. This includes:

a £3,000 setting up home allowance for essential household items

support to purchase contents insurance and TV licences

full council tax exemption until age 25 for those living in Derbyshire (with the Leaving Care Service covering this for those living elsewhere)

Care leavers are also supported with:

budgeting sessions

tenancy‑readiness tools such as the Resettlement Passport

help to access their junior ISA

tailored support to ensure they are better off in work, including bridging payments while awaiting Universal Credit and discounts such as reduced water bills or temporary free Wi‑Fi

Legal duties

This section outlines the legal duties each local authority should consider as part of the local offer.

It includes details on:

corporate parenting, which includes a regional approach to the local offer

personal adviser support post-21

Staying Close support

domestic abuse

Corporate parenting

Every local authority is a corporate parent. The local offer is the clear, public statement of how these corporate parenting duties translate into practical, day-to-day support for care-experienced young people across areas such as housing, health, education, employment and participation.

Local authorities may wish to consider a regional approach to their local offer to ensure consistency in their corporate parenting duties and the support they offer to their care-experienced young people.

Corporate parenting principles includes further information.

passages.quote:
l authorities should:

consider how they are helping young people develop and sustain enduring relationships

strengthen their sense of belonging

support them to access lifelong networks of support that continue beyond formal statutory involvement

This expectation is underpinned by the Children’s social care national framework, which sets out the outcomes that local authorities should achieve for children, young people and families. It outlines that children in care and care leavers should have stable, loving homes, and that local authorities should help care leavers to build and sustain loving relationships with family and friends.

Principles underpinning the local offer

The local offer should be underpinned by a recognition that building and sustaining loving relationships around care leavers should be the key focus of services working with them. Local offers should therefore not only describe the services available to young people but also how those services will help them build, maintain and strengthen the relationships, networks and community connections that enable them to thrive throughout adulthood.

The local offer must provide information on all services available to care-experienced young people from the local authority and, where relevant, from partner agencies, including specific arrangements for supporting and assisting care-experienced young people in:

their transition to adulthood

accommodation

financial support

access to services

This includes details of statutory entitlements as well as any discretionary support that the local authority chooses to provide.

In determining the discretionary elements of the local offer, local authorities may wish to consider whether certain forms of support could be extended to qualifying care leavers and to other young people with experience of care, including those living in kinship care.

In developing their local offer, local authorities should have regard to the Children’s Commissioner’s Hierarchy of needs for care-experienced young people, acknowledging that a sense of belonging, a positive identity, trusted and enduring relationships and meaningful participation are key foundations for young people to thrive and achieve positive lifelong outcomes.

Corporate parenting principles

Under Section 1 of the Children and Social Work Act 2017, local authorities are required to have regard to 7 corporate parenting principles when exercising their functions in relation to looked after children and care-experienced young people.

The local offer should:

explain the support available from all local authority departments, not just children’s services or care leaver teams, and show how this support aligns with the 7 corporate parenting principles in Section 1 of the Children and Social Work Act 2017

be developed jointly with care-experienced young people and reflect the 7 principles

These principles should underpin the development and implementation of the local offer and should be read alongside this guidance.

In particular, local authorities should recognise the importance of promoting stable, loving and enduring relationships and ensuring that care-experienced young people have trusted adults and supportive networks that extend beyond specific services or interventions.

Corporate parenting includes further information and a case study.

Who this guidance is for

This guidance is for local authorities and partner organisations that contribute to services and support for care-experienced young people, including:

county councils, district councils and London borough councils

Combined County Authorities and the Greater London Authority

housing authorities and housing associations

health partners, such as NHS services, GPs, mental health providers and universal health services relevant to a care-experienced young person

education, training and skills providers, including further education (FE) colleges, higher education (HE) institutions, independent training providers, careers services and training bodies

employment partners, including Jobcentre Plus, the Department for Work and Pensions and employers offering apprenticeships or ring-fenced roles for a care-experienced young person

voluntary and community sector organisations providing mentoring, wellbeing, participation or specialist support

youth justice, prison and probation services, where relevant to a care-experienced young person’s needs

All local authorities in England are required to publish a local offer.

For the purpose of this guidance, a local authority in England means:

a county council in England

a district council

a London borough council

the Common Council, of the City of London (in their capacity as a local authority)

the Council of the Isles of Scilly

a combined authority established under section 103 of the Local Democracy, Economic Development and Construction Act 2009

Housing and accommodation

This section includes details on:

accommodation planning

working with housing services

preventing homelessness

support for young people leaving custody

additional support

working as part of a regional care cooperative

Local authorities must publish information about how they:

anticipate the future accommodation needs of care-experienced young people, both before the young person leaves care and on an ongoing basis once they have left care

co-operate with local housing authorities in their area to assist former relevant children aged under 25 to find and keep suitable accommodation

provide assistance to former relevant children under 25 who are at risk of homelessness or leaving custody (where they have been detained in prison, a young offender institution or a secure training centre)

Accommodation planning

The local offer should explain:

how the local authority assesses and plans for the accommodation needs of care-experienced young people

the accommodation options available locally and how to access them
